subject: Computer Networking
title: Mobile Data: How Phones Use the Internet
description: A quick, practical guide to Mobile Data: How Phones Use the Internet.

hook.text: You open an app on the bus. Data flows through cell towers, fiber cables, and servers in milliseconds.

buildup.text: Your phone connects to a nearby tower. The tower connects to the carrier's core network via fiber.

discovery.text: The core network routes your request to the internet. It also handles billing, security, and quality of service.

twist.text: Mobile data goes through more hops than Wi-Fi. That extra path adds latency — which is why Wi-Fi often feels faster.

climax.text: Carrier aggregation bonds multiple frequency bands together for faster speeds. Your phone uses several bands at once.

punchline.text: Mobile data is wireless at the edge, wired at the core.

quiz.question: What is carrier aggregation?
options: Combining multiple frequency bands for faster speeds
Switching between Wi-Fi and cellular automatically
Routing traffic through multiple cell towers simultaneously

details.summary: Mobile data connects phones to the internet through cellular networks using a packet data network gateway that bridges the cellular and IP networks.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the mobile data path explains why cellular latency differs from Wi-Fi, how carrier networks manage traffic, and what affects mobile internet performance.
takeaways: Phones receive IP addresses from the carrier's core network
Data traverses the radio network, core network, then the internet
Carrier-Grade NAT shares public IPs among many mobile devices

faq.question: Why is cellular latency higher than Wi-Fi?
faq.answer: Cellular data travels from the phone to the tower, through the carrier's transport and core networks, then to the internet. This path is longer than Wi-Fi's direct route through a local router. Radio scheduling, handoffs, and core network processing add milliseconds.

faq.question: What is Carrier-Grade NAT?
faq.answer: Carriers have more subscribers than available public IPv4 addresses. Carrier-Grade NAT shares a single public IP among many devices, each getting a private address. This adds a layer of address translation that can complicate peer-to-peer connections, gaming, and VPN usage on mobile networks.
